answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: Douglass wrote this in his first autobiography, Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, an American Slave (1845), Chapter V — reflecting on his move from Colonel Lloyd’s plantation to Baltimore as a “special interposition of divine Providence.” The wording is confirmed against the primary text.

source.heading: The documented source

docMeta.dd: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, an American Slave

source.excerpt: I may be deemed superstitious, and even egotistical, in regarding this event as a special interposition of divine Providence in my favor. But I should be false to the earliest sentiments of my soul, if I suppressed the opinion. I prefer to be true to myself, even at the hazard of incurring the ridicule of others, rather than to be false, and incur my own abhorrence.
trail: Wikiquote ↗ lists the line in its Sourced section, citing the 1845 Narrative, Chapter V.
We then confirmed it word-for-word against the primary text of the Narrative at Project Gutenberg ↗, where it sits in the Baltimore / “divine Providence” passage of Chapter V.
The popular circulated wording adds a stray “to” (“and to incur my own abhorrence”); Douglass’s printed text reads simply “and incur my own abhorrence.”
source.excerptNote: The “event” Douglass means is his selection, as a boy, to leave Colonel Lloyd’s plantation for Baltimore — which he read as a providential turning point in his life.

author.name: Frederick Douglass
author.heading: About Frederick Douglass
author.bio: Born into slavery in Maryland around 1818, Frederick Douglass escaped in 1838 and became the most influential Black abolitionist of the nineteenth century — a spellbinding orator, newspaper editor, and adviser to presidents. His 1845 Narrative was a bestselling autobiography that put a devastating first-person face on American slavery. He later expanded his life story in My Bondage and My Freedom (1855) and Life and Times of Frederick Douglass (1881).

misattribution.heading: One thing to get right
misattribution.intro: The attribution to Frederick Douglass is correct — this really is his line. The only thing worth flagging is a small wording drift in how it’s usually quoted.

items.why: Most reprints read “rather than to be false, and to incur my own abhorrence.” Douglass’s printed 1845 text has no second “to”: “and incur my own abhorrence,” per the Narrative ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: Genuine Douglass, from Chapter V of the 1845 Narrative ↗ — just quote it without the extra “to.”

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The sentence comes at a hinge point in Douglass’s story: as a boy he was chosen to leave the plantation for Baltimore, a move he later saw as the opening that made his eventual freedom possible. Bracing for readers who would call him “superstitious” or “egotistical” for reading Providence into his own life, he plants his flag: he would rather risk ridicule than betray “the earliest sentiments of my soul.”
